item.title: CNMI tourism groups press for EVS-TAP reinstatement as China market powers visitor gains
item.description: Tourism and business leaders are urging the federal government to restore a key travel authorization program for Chinese visitors, warning that its suspension could undermine the Commonwealth's fragile economic recovery just as visitor arrivals show signs of improvement. item.content:encoded:
Tourism and business leaders are urging the federal government to restore a key travel authorization program for Chinese visitors, warning that its suspension could undermine the Commonwealth's fragile economic recovery just as visitor arrivals show signs of improvement.

The Marianas Visitors Authority, the Hotel Association of the Northern Mariana Islands and the Saipan Chamber of Commerce this week voiced concern over the U.S. Department of Homeland Security's decision to suspend the CNMI Economic Vitality and Security Travel Authorization Program, or EVS-TAP, effective Oct. 30. The program allows eligible, pre-screened Chinese nationals to travel to the CNMI without obtaining a U.S. visa.

DHS said the suspension is based on national security and immigration-enforcement concerns, citing alleged vulnerabilities involving travel by Chinese nationals, including overstays, illegal employment and other abuses of federal immigration programs.

Local tourism leaders argue the program has become an essential economic lifeline for the CNMI and contend that many incidents cited by DHS predate EVS-TAP's implementation in 2025.

The debate comes as the CNMI continues to struggle with a slow tourism recovery following Super Typhoon Sinlaku. Industry leaders say the loss of EVS-TAP could reduce passenger demand on international routes linking Saipan with Hong Kong and South Korea, threatening already limited airline service and the broader visitor economy.

MVA Acting Board Chair Vicky Benavente said Chinese visitors accounted for more than 20% of total arrivals during fiscal 2026.

"The security of the Commonwealth of the Northern Mariana Islands and our nation must always be protected," Benavente said. "National security and economic security go hand in hand."

HANMI Chairman Ivan Quichocho described the suspension as "devastating" for hotels and tourism businesses already dealing with reduced visitor arrivals, limited airline capacity and rising costs. He said Chinese visitors make up a significant share of passengers traveling on routes connecting the CNMI with Hong Kong and South Korea and warned that losing those travelers could weaken the viability of flights serving multiple markets.

The Saipan Chamber of Commerce similarly cautioned that the economic effects would extend far beyond the tourism industry, affecting restaurants, retailers, transportation providers, tax collections and public services. The chamber called on DHS to work with CNMI leaders to identify additional safeguards rather than eliminating the program altogether.

The concerns come as MVA reported modest improvement in visitor arrivals. The CNMI welcomed 5,051 visitors in September, slightly higher than August's total.

China became the CNMI's largest source market during the month, posting 1,328 arrivals, a 95% increase from 680 visitors in September 2025. For fiscal 2026, arrivals from China rose 20% compared with the previous fiscal year.

Overall arrivals, however, remain well below previous levels. September's total was down 30% from the 7,266 visitors recorded a year earlier, while fiscal 2026 arrivals fell 38% to 99,476 from 160,640 in fiscal 2025.

South Korea generated 1,137 arrivals in September, followed by the United States with 1,239 visitors, Japan with 444, Guam with 618 and other markets with 285.

MVA said rebuilding airline capacity remains critical to recovery. Jeju Air currently operates four weekly flights between Seoul and Saipan, United Airlines maintains service from Tokyo and Guam, and Philippine Airlines recently resumed nonstop Manila-Saipan flights.

Tourism officials say restoring EVS-TAP could prove equally important as the CNMI works to rebuild visitor numbers, preserve international air links and support an economy still heavily dependent on tourism.

item.title: Palau Visitors Authority reports 76% tourism recovery from pre-pandemic levels
item.description: Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels. There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.
item.content:encoded:
Palau Visitors Authority is reporting a 76% recovery in visitor arrivals compared with pre-pandemic levels.

There were 71,681 visitors last year, compared with 93,723 in 2019.

As of September, 63,948 people had traveled to Palau, meaning the country is on track to exceed last year’s total arrivals.

The Visitors Authority says that in 2025, Palau recorded the highest number of American, Australian and European tourists in the nation’s history. China remained Palau’s top visitor source market, with Taiwan ranking second.

The average visitor stay in Palau was a record 5.9 nights in 2025.

item.title: PBS Guam to host annual pledge drive Saturday
item.description: PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday. The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.
item.content:encoded:
PBS Guam will host its annual Pledge Drive, “The Story Continues,” on Saturday.

The broadcast will feature local performances, previews of upcoming local programs, and updates on returning shows.

The annual fundraiser supports PBS Guam’s educational, cultural, and locally produced programming. The station relies on contributions from viewers, government, and foundations to continue providing educational content and sharing Guam’s stories.

PBS Guam is offering pledge gifts based on donation amounts. Donors who contribute $75 will receive a PBS Guam merchandise mystery box. A $100 donation includes a windbreaker, tote bag, director’s hat, and one year of PBS Passport access. A $150 donation includes all four gifts and one year of PBS Passport access, which provides an on-demand library of PBS programs, shows, and documentaries.

The pledge drive will air on KGTF Channel 12 and stream through the PBS App and YouTube at youtube.com/pbsguam . Rebroadcasts will air on KGTF Channel 12 every Sunday evening throughout Nov.

Community members can donate online at pbsguam.org/support or call 671-734-5483 for more information.

item.title: 9 dead as jet nosedives and erupts into fireball near busy roadway in South Florida
item.description: A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation's transportation secretary said. Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Pal
item.content:encoded:
A business jet carrying nine people nose-dived into a South Florida neighborhood Sunday and erupted into a giant fireball that appeared to just miss homes near a busy roadway. Everyone on board was killed, the nation's transportation secretary said.

Video recorded by people inside their cars captured the terrifying moment the Bahamas-bound aircraft plunged from the sky before striking near the Palm Beach County roadway and exploding. Flames flickered around chunks of pavement lining a crater as people milled about, expressing shock that it landed only feet from homes and inches from passing vehicles. Thick black smoke engulfed the crash site.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy posted on X that the Learjet 60 crashed in Palm Beach County at 12:50 p.m. and called it a "horrific tragedy." The Federal Aviation Administration is sending a team to support the National Transportation Safety Board's investigation, he said.

Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis said there were no immediate reports of anyone on the ground injured or killed.

"It was a cataclysmic plane crash," DeSantis told reporters at the scene. "It looked like a missile going down and left a big crater on the side of the road."

Rain pounded the region on Sunday. A flood watch due to excessive rainfall was in effect through Monday afternoon, the National Weather Service said.

The aircraft had departed Austin-Bergstrom International Airport in Texas and was headed to the Bahamas, according to the Federal Aviation Administration. Authorities did not immediately say what caused the jet to go down or who was on it.

The plane was heading east at 35,000 feet (about 11 kilometers) when pilots reported turbulence, icing and precipitation and requested to climb another 2,000 feet (about 610 meters).

Moments later, the plane entered a steep dive, first 10,000 feet per minute, then 20,000 feet per minute and up to 30,000 feet per minute, speeding the plane beyond its design limits, according to air traffic control recordings and flight tracking data.

A pilot declared an emergency and issued distress calls. The plane banked sharply to the right before it smashed into the ground.

Minutes before the crash, the pilot reported ice accumulating on the jet and turbulence that was jolting it by as much as 700 feet (213 meters), according to air traffic control recordings captured by LiveATC.net.

"We have light, clear ice that is manageable and moderate turbulence," the pilot told controllers.

But the situation rapidly deteriorated. After encountering precipitation and requesting to climb, the pilot declared an emergency as the aircraft began losing altitude at an alarming rate.

"We're descending 8,000 – mayday, mayday - we're descending 10,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed.

"We are in an overspeed condition descending 20,000 feet per minute," the pilot radioed, before delivering a devastating acknowledgment of what was about to happen. "We're going to crash into the ground."

Jim Reynolds, a spokesperson for Austin-Bergstrom International Airport, said the jet was a private aircraft. He could not immediately provide details about who was on the flight.

Steve Arroyo, an aviation safety expert, said icing and turbulence could have been factors in the crash and may have caused the plane to stall while it was cruising at 34,000 feet (10,363 meters).

There are many potential factors and the NTSB will consider all of them, including how the pilot responded to the icing and turbulence reported over the radio. But investigators won't rule anything out at this early stage, he said.

The NTSB said investigators were expected to arrive at the crash site on Sunday and Monday. A media briefing is scheduled for Monday in West Palm Beach.

Palm Beach County authorities were evacuating about 600 people from a nearby mobile home community while federal officials investigate the crash. The road will be closed until further notice, county officials said.

The crash occurred in Greenacres, Florida, according to Palm Beach County sheriff's officials. The city of 45,000 people is about 7 miles (11 kilometers) southwest of West Palm Beach.

item.title: Do you know signs of a stroke? BE FAST are the words to remember
item.description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke. The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., suffered a stroke on Saturday. His prognosis is excellent, according to his office. His case illustrates the importance of knowing the warning signs of a stroke.

The American Stroke Association says following the six letters in the acronym BE FAST — can help save stroke victims and prevent permanent brain damage.

Murphy, 53, had the "A" for "arm weakness" — he felt numbness in his arm while he was at his son's hockey game, according to a statement from his staff. And they said he acted quickly to get care — that's the "T" for "time."

Being seen by medical professionals as soon as possible — be fast! — gives people the best shot at survival and full recovery.

Here are all six of the stroke-spotting signs in the BE FAST acronym, according to the American Stroke Association:

Dizzyness, trouble walking or a sudden loss of balance are all signs that a stroke may be occurring.

Is the person having trouble with their vision? Blurred vision, double vision or loss of sight in one eye are important symptoms.

Ask the person to smile. Is their smile uneven? Numbness or drooping on one side of the face is a symptom.

Numbness in one arm, as Murphy had, is a symptom. Weakness is too. Ask the person to raise both arms. Does one arm drift down?

Trouble talking is another common symptom. Can the person repeat a simple sentence? Is their speech slurred or hard to understand?

If you or someone you are with is experiencing these symptoms, call 911 as soon as you can. Getting care quickly is very important for survival and to minimize long-term effects.

A stroke happens when blood flow to or within the brain is interrupted. It can happen when an artery is blocked or when a blood vessel in the brain bursts. Brain tissue that is deprived of oxygen can be permanently damaged, resulting in long-term disability or death.

Other important symptoms of a stroke are a severe headache, confusion and numbness on one side of the body.

Stroke is the #4 leading cause of death in the U.S., killing more than 162,000 people in 2023, according to the American Heart Association.

item.title: Haley Stevens endorses GOP candidate in Michigan Senate race, spurning Abdul El-Sayed

Haley Stevens has endorsed GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her former primary rival Abdul El-Sayed, less than 48 hours before Election Day. item.content:encoded:
DETROIT — After months of proclaiming support for the Democratic ticket, Rep. Haley Stevens has endorsed GOP Michigan Senate candidate Mike Rogers over her former primary rival Abdul El-Sayed, less than 48 hours before Election Day.

"As you may have seen, our Democratic nominee for U.S. Senate, Abdul, said I was no longer welcome in his campaign and that I should stay away, and he's right," Stevens said in a video she posted to social media on Sunday. "And that's why I am endorsing Mike Rogers for the U.S. Senate today."

Her statement followed a surprise appearance with Rogers at a church in Detroit.

Outside a "Souls to the Polls" event at a church in Detroit, El-Sayed told reporters that he doesn't think about Stevens and said voters do not either.

"None of this matters," El-Sayed said. "You know what matters. You can go, like, 15 minutes that way, or 15 minutes that way, or 15 minutes that way. And there are families who are preparing to send their kids to schools tomorrow that look like they did 50 years ago. They're worried about what they're going to feed their kids for lunch. They're worried that if one of their kids gets sick, they're not going to be able to pay the bills."

In her endorsement, Stevens said she does "not stand with Hasan Piker," a streamer that El-Sayed campaigned with during the primary. In August, after Piker implied that Jews' support for Israel puts them at risk of personal violence, El-Sayed sought to distance himself from the controversy, saying Piker did not speak for the campaign. He stopped short of disavowing Piker.

Stevens had been critical that El-Sayed was not doing enough to reassure Jewish and Black voters who supported her during the primary. Even though relations between the pair had been publicly disintegrating for weeks, Stevens' announcement was a surprise.

Tensions accelerated after Stevens' fiance, Jason Turkish, said he planned to vote for Rogers. In a subsequent TV appearance, Stevens maintained she was still planning to support the Democratic nominee. She urged El-Sayed to denounce a recent ad by Cenk Uygur, of Young Turks, that blamed Israel for high grocery prices in the United States.

"The ad tells Michigan families they cannot afford groceries because their money has to be set aside 'for killing Palestinians,' and it blames our close ally Israel for everything Michiganders cannot afford," she wrote.

El-Sayed's campaign had said he had nothing to do with the ad and criticized the contents of the ad on Saturday.

Stevens said she was originally scheduled to attend a different church event in Detroit on Sunday alongside El-Sayed and Rep. James Clyburn, D-S.C. The planned joint appearance was meant to be a unifying event for the party ahead of the election. But on Friday, Stevens set a condition for her participation in the event — that El-Sayed reject the ad and apologize for rhetoric she considered to be inflammatory and offensive.

The event with El-Sayed and Clyburn went ahead as planned, without Stevens.

Stevens' announcement has sent shockwaves through the Democratic Party.

Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., called it a "despicable betrayal."

"Haley Stevens' decision to campaign with Rogers — a man who has repeatedly sold out Michigan's working class, wants to pass a national abortion ban, and has pledged to be a loyal vote for Trump's agenda — shows that she has abandoned everything she claims to care about," Michigan Democratic Party Chair Curtis Hertel said in a statement.

Stevens' communications director has an email auto reply that says as of Sunday, he is no longer working for the Stevens office. On social media, several former campaign staffers slammed their former boss' actions.

The clash between the two Michigan Democrats highlights a broader rift within the party as it relates to Israel and rhetoric around Israel. That schism is likely to extend far beyond Election Day and will be something the Democratic Party has to contend with, particularly as it prepares for the 2028 presidential nominating process.

item.title: Connecticut Senator Chris Murphy is hospitalized with a stroke
item.description: Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., has been hospitalized following a stroke, according to his office. In a statement on Sunday, Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said he is expected to make a full recovery.
item.content:encoded:
Sen. Chris Murphy, D-Conn., has been hospitalized following a stroke, according to his office.

In a statement on Sunday, Murphy's chief of staff, Allison Herwitt, said he is expected to make a full recovery.

"Yesterday afternoon, Senator Murphy started experiencing numbness in his arm while at his son's hockey game," Herwitt wrote. "He was taken to a local hospital, where it was discovered he had experienced a stroke. He was transferred to Johns Hopkins for further monitoring and is responding well to treatment."

Murphy, 53, is a prominent figure in the party and has been a prolific campaign surrogate for candidates through the midterm cycle. Viewed as a possible 2028 presidential contender, Murphy has carved out a position as a foreign policy leader and champion of aggressive executive branch oversight.

He recently returned from a multistop tour in the Middle East, after which he warned that President Trump would dramatically escalate his war on Iran after the midterm election.

The lawmaker is the latest in a string of lawmakers to experience a health crisis this year. Sen. Mitch McConnell, R-Ky., missed months of Senate work during a lengthy hospital stay and rehabilitation process. Rep. Tom Kean, R-N.J., was missing from the Capitol for months for what he later announced was treatment for depression.

In 2022, three prominent Democratic lawmakers — Sen. Ben Ray Lujan of New Mexico, Chis Van Hollen of Maryland, and then-Senate candidate John Fetterman — were all hospitalized for strokes.
